results.summary: Toy CPU is an 8-bit accumulator-based processor with a small instruction set, designed for the Tiny Tapeout platform. It accepts instructions serially through the 6-bit input pins, using a start sequence to begin execution, and outputs data on 8 output pins. The design is intended for educational purposes and simple experimentation, requiring an external clock and reset signal. It is a minimal CPU implementation that demonstrates basic computer architecture concepts.

This design counts from 0 to 9 at one-second intervals, displaying the count on a 7-segment display. It uses a clock divider to generate the one-second timing from the 1000 Hz input clock and includes combinational logic for binary-to-decimal conversion. A slower square wave is also output on pin 7. The project serves as a simple test or demonstration of timing and display functionality.

QTCore-A1 is an 8-bit accumulator-based microprocessor with a Von Neumann architecture, designed through GPT-4 conversations. It uses an SPI interface for loading programs and controlling execution via a scan chain, allowing an external microcontroller to read and write processor state. The design includes a small instruction set and an assembler, and it can be synthesized to FPGAs. Notable for being entirely generated by GPT-4, it serves as an educational example of AI-assisted hardware design.

This design creates a moving light effect similar to the Knight Rider sensor lights, using shift registers and counters. It provides speed and brightness control via input pins, with brightness achieved through PWM at 50 Hz. The outputs are intended to drive LEDs with series resistors, and push buttons can be connected to the control inputs. It is a simple visual effect generator for entertainment or display purposes.

This is a logic-locked version of the QTCore-A1 8-bit microprocessor, where parts of the ALU, control unit, and instruction decoding are locked using a key. The correct key must be provided in the program for the processor to function, and it is loaded via the scan chain. The design includes a 7-segment display driver and uses SPI for program loading and execution. It demonstrates RTL locking techniques for hardware security.

This design implements a two-channel XOR stream cipher using programmable 32-bit Galois LFSRs for encryption and decryption. It can be configured via a 130-bit serial shift register to set LFSR taps and state, and it supports simultaneous transmit and receive channels. The default configuration uses PRBS-31 taps and a fixed state. It is intended for secure communication experiments and requires external hardware for testing.

This circuit converts 5-bit Baudot code from a teletype machine to 8-bit ASCII. It uses two UARTs, a clock divider, and a conversion ROM to handle the data conversion. The design requires an optoisolator at the Baudot input and a USB serial adapter at the ASCII output. It is useful for interfacing vintage teletype equipment with modern serial devices.

This is a two-player game where players compete to press their button first after a countdown. The countdown and winner are displayed on LEDs. It uses a finite state machine and counters, and requires external pushbuttons and LEDs for operation. The design is educational, demonstrating basic digital logic and game mechanics.

This design stores and outputs the first 1400 decimal digits of Pi to a 7-segment display using densely packed decimal encoding. It uses an index counter to select digits and includes a decimal point. The design is an experiment in data storage and display, and it requires a 7-segment display for output. It is notable for its efficient use of area to store a large number of digits.

This design plays the Super Mario theme tune through a piezo speaker using differential PWM modulation. It converts an RTTL ringtone into Verilog and outputs the sound wave on two pins. The design requires a piezo speaker connected across the output pins and a 6.25 kHz clock. It is a simple music player for entertainment purposes.
